report:
**Conclusion: broadly, yes—your “no” is the best current practical answer.** Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) has *not* been shown reliably to relieve statin-related muscle discomfort, so it should not be considered a proven treatment.

Why the evidence is unconvincing:

- The most informative randomized trial first verified that participants’ pain actually occurred with simvastatin rather than placebo. In that selected group, CoQ10 did **not** reduce muscle pain, improve strength, or improve aerobic performance. This matters because many reported “statin” muscle symptoms have other causes or occur on placebo too.  
  https://www.atherosclerosis-journal.com/article/S0021-9150(14)01636-0/fulltext

- A 2020 systematic review/meta-analysis concluded CoQ10 did **not** improve statin-associated muscle pain or adherence to statin treatment.  
  https://www.endocrinologyadvisor.com/news/coq10-therapy-may-not-improve-statin-adherence-or-relieve-associated-muscle-pain-in-statin-associated-myalgia/

- Evidence is mixed: a 2018 meta-analysis of small trials reported symptom improvement, but variation in symptom definitions, statin regimens, and study quality limits confidence in that result.  
  https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30371340/

The biological rationale is plausible—statins can affect the pathway that produces CoQ10—but a plausible mechanism is not proof that supplementation helps symptoms. Discuss new muscle pain with the prescriber rather than stopping a statin yourself; evaluating other causes and trying a different dose/statin or evidence-based nonstatin lipid treatment may be more useful.
